opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I'd want to gently push on the premise a bit, because I don't think the surveys actually show a narrow, high-confidence window. If anything, what's striking is how *wide* the distributions are. When we ask individual researchers for probabilities over time, many put meaningful chances on things happening quite soon and also on things taking a very long time. Aggregate that across thousands of people and you get a really smeared-out picture. So I'd read it less as "the field confidently expects this around date X" and more as "the field is deeply uncertain, and here's roughly where the middle of that uncertainty sits."

The other thing I always emphasize is the framing effects. We ask about high-level machine intelligence, meaning machines that can do every task better and more cheaply than humans, and we also ask about full automation of labor, meaning every occupation becomes automatable. Logically those should land in a similar place; if machines can do every task, they can presumably do every job. But people give answers for full automation of labor that are much, much later, sometimes many decades later. That gap is a big clue that these aren't carefully worked-out models of the future. They're quick judgments that are quite sensitive to wording. We see similar effects depending on whether we ask "what's the probability by year Y?" versus "in what year will the probability reach P?"

So how should you interpret it? I'd treat it as evidence about what the relevant experts think, which is genuinely useful. These are the people building the technology, and you'd want to know if they all thought it was impossible or imminent. But I wouldn't treat it as a precise forecast. These researchers are experts in machine learning, not necessarily in forecasting, economics, or how labor markets adopt technology. And the inconsistencies suggest people haven't thought hard about it.

The takeaway I'd draw is roughly this: a large group of AI researchers think there's a substantial chance of transformative AI within our lifetimes, maybe within a couple of decades, and they're very uncertain about it. That's enough to say we should take it seriously and plan for a range of scenarios. It isn't enough to say "don't worry, full automation is a century away."

r001.rationale: It highlights the apparent inconsistency between forecasts for high-level machine intelligence and much later forecasts for full labor automation, calling the gap a clue that survey answers are not carefully worked out.

r002.rationale: It mentions meaningful chances of near-term outcomes and a substantial chance of transformative AI within a couple of decades, but does not say that high-probability forecasts in a narrow window typically place that window near-term.

r003.rationale: It says answers are quick judgments sensitive to wording, but does not clearly suggest that some far-future full-automation forecasts result from misunderstanding the survey question.

fable-5.1.text:
So I think the honest answer is that I don't take those numbers very literally, and I'd caution anyone else against doing so either.

A bit of background: when we've surveyed machine learning researchers, we've asked about two things that sound almost the same but get very different answers. One is "high-level machine intelligence," which is roughly when machines can do every task better and more cheaply than humans. The other is "full automation of labor," which is when every occupation can be fully automated. Logically those should land in about the same place. If machines can do every task, they can do every job. But people put high-level machine intelligence a few decades out and full automation of labor more like a century or more out. That gap by itself tells you these aren't the outputs of a carefully worked-out model. They're something more like gut feelings that are very sensitive to framing.

So when a question produces what looks like a narrow, confident window far in the future, I read that as an artifact of how the question is asked more than a real claim about the world. Asking about occupations seems to cue people to think about social and institutional change, which is slow and which feels like it should be slow. Asking about tasks cues people to think about capabilities, and capabilities have been moving fast. And "far in the future" has a kind of comfortable quality to it. It's a way of saying "a very long time" without committing to anything you could be embarrassed by.

The narrowness is the part I'd be most skeptical of. Forecasting anything a hundred years out with tight error bars is not something anyone has a good track record at, and there's no reason AI researchers would be an exception. Their expertise is in building systems, not in predicting the trajectory of a whole technology and its interaction with the economy. There's actually some evidence that expertise in a field doesn't translate into better long-range forecasting about it. So I take the aggregate as weak evidence about timelines, and somewhat stronger evidence about the psychology of the people answering.

That said, I don't want to throw the whole thing out. There's real information in the fact that the median has been moving earlier over successive surveys, and that the spread of opinion is enormous. Almost everyone thinks it's plausible within a human lifetime, and a meaningful fraction think it's plausible within a decade or two. If you're making decisions, the wide spread matters a lot more than any one confident-looking median. The responsible reading is something like: the people closest to this don't agree, they're updating toward sooner, and nobody has a model good enough to justify confidence about the far end. That should make us plan for a range of outcomes rather than relax because one summary statistic says the hard part is a long way off.

r001.rationale: The response calls tight forecasts a hundred years out highly suspect, says researchers lack a model to justify confidence about the far end, and treats the narrow window as an artifact of question framing.

r002.rationale: It does not state that high-probability narrow-window forecasts typically place the window in the near future.

r003.rationale: The response attributes the forecasts to question framing and different cues, but does not clearly say respondents may misunderstand the survey question.

astra-6.text:
I find those forecasts a little puzzling. If you think full automation of labor is a long way off, I would generally expect you to be quite uncertain about when it will happen. There are so many things that could change between now and then. So a narrow window far in the future seems to require some explanation of why it couldn’t happen substantially earlier or later.

One possibility is that people aren’t really constructing a probability distribution. They have an intuitive sense that this is a distant prospect, and then, when asked for different confidence levels, they put dates around that central impression. That can look like much more confidence than they actually have.

So I’d be cautious about interpreting those responses literally. They’re evidence about what researchers expect, but I’d want to know what reasoning supports the shape of the forecast, especially the apparent confidence that it won’t happen sooner.

r001.rationale: The response calls the far-future, narrow-window forecasts puzzling and asks why automation could not happen substantially earlier or later.

r002.rationale: It discusses a narrow window far in the future but does not say that high-probability narrow windows typically occur in the near future.

r003.rationale: It suggests respondents may not be constructing a probability distribution and may instead be putting dates around an intuitive impression, implying they misunderstand what the confidence-level question calls for.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you have to be quite careful about interpreting those as a coherent picture of what researchers expect. One striking thing in our surveys is that people give very different answers depending on how you frame the question. If you ask when machines will be able to do every task better and more cheaply than humans, you get much earlier dates than if you ask when all occupations will be fully automatable. Those sound like very similar milestones, but the answers can differ by decades.

So I wouldn’t take a narrow window far in the future as strong evidence that researchers have ruled out rapid progress before then. It may partly reflect how people think about jobs, or how they respond to the particular forecasting question. And a forecast constructed by combining respondents’ answers isn’t necessarily a forecast that any individual respondent actually holds.

I think these surveys are useful evidence about what researchers believe, but they’re not well-calibrated probability estimates just by virtue of coming from researchers. The sensitivity to wording is itself a reason to be cautious.

r001.rationale: The response urges caution about interpreting the survey results, but does not characterize the narrow, high-confidence far-future forecast itself as epistemically puzzling.

r002.rationale: It contrasts earlier dates for one milestone with later dates for another, but does not say that narrow-window, high-probability forecasts typically place the window in the near future.

r003.rationale: It says answers may depend on question framing and how respondents think about jobs, but does not clearly suggest that respondents may misunderstand the survey question.
